readings.title: First reading
readings.text:
The stream in the place where Elijah lay hidden dried up, for the country had no rain. And then the word of the Lord came to Elijah, ‘Up and go to Zarephath, a Sidonian town, and stay there. I have ordered a widow there to give you food.’ So he went off to Sidon. And when he reached the city gate, there was a widow gathering sticks; addressing her he said, ‘Please bring me a little water in a vessel for me to drink.’ She was setting off to bring it when he called after her. ‘Please’ he said ‘bring me a scrap of bread in your hand.’ ‘As the Lord your God lives,’ she replied ‘I have no baked bread, but only a handful of meal in a jar and a little oil in a jug; I am just gathering a stick or two to go and prepare this for myself and my son to eat, and then we shall die.’ But Elijah said to her, ‘Do not be afraid, go and do as you have said; but first make a little scone of it for me and bring it to me, and then make some for yourself and for your son. For thus the Lord speaks, the God of Israel:
“Jar of meal shall not be spent,
jug of oil shall not be emptied,
before the day when the Lord sends
rain on the face of the earth.”’
The woman went and did as Elijah told her and they ate the food, she, himself and her son. The jar of meal was not spent nor the jug of oil emptied, just as the Lord had foretold through Elijah.

exegesis.summary: In the midst of a devastating drought, the Lord sends Elijah not to the rich of Israel but to a destitute pagan widow in Sidon, asking her to give from her last scrap of meal and oil. Her act of faith—feeding the prophet before her own starving son—unleashes a miracle of unfailing provision: the jar of meal is not spent, nor the jug of oil emptied. This is a foreshadowing of God's hidden abundance for those who trust His word above their fear.

patristicQuotes.quote: Elias fed the woman, but gave her just what was enough for her; but Jesus, being the Lord, makes His gifts with superabundant profusion.

A friend comes to you on his journey, that is, in this present life, in which all are travelling on as strangers... He delays to give, wishing that you should the more earnestly desire what is delayed.

cccReferences.title: Elijah teaches the widow of Zarephath to believe

exegesis.thematicConnection: The widow's tiny portion that does not run out anticipates the Gospel's salt and light: a small thing, faithfully given, becomes a sign that nourishes and illumines the world.

readings.title: Responsorial Psalm
readings.text:
Lift up the light of your face on us, O Lord.
When I call, answer me, O God of justice;
from anguish you released me, have mercy and hear me!
O men, how long will your hearts be closed,
will you love what is futile and seek what is false?
Lift up the light of your face on us, O Lord.
It is the Lord who grants favours to those whom he loves;
the Lord hears me whenever I call him.
Fear him; do not sin: ponder on your bed and be still.
Lift up the light of your face on us, O Lord.
‘What can bring us happiness?’ many say.
Lift up the light of your face on us, O Lord.
You have put into my heart a greater joy
than they have from abundance of corn and new wine.
Lift up the light of your face on us, O Lord.
readings.refrain: Lift up the light of your face on us, O Lord.

exegesis.summary: The psalmist cries out for God to lift the light of His face upon His people, confessing that true joy is not found in abundant harvests but in the Lord Himself. It is the prayer of one who has tasted God's mercy in anguish and now urges others to turn from what is futile.

patristicQuotes.quote: To lift up our heads is to raise up our minds to the joys of the heavenly country.

cccReferences.title: Our heart is restless until it rests in You
Love as the source of prayer

exegesis.thematicConnection: The widow of Zarephath learns that joy is not in the meal-jar's reserve but in trusting the God who shines His face upon her; the disciples in the Gospel are sent to be that very light.

readings.title: Gospel
readings.text: Jesus said to his disciples: ‘You are the salt of the earth. But if salt becomes tasteless, what can make it salty again? It is good for nothing, and can only be thrown out to be trampled underfoot by men.

exegesis.summary: Jesus addresses His disciples on the mountain with a stunning vocation: they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Like salt, they must preserve the world from decay and give it savor through the witness of holy lives; if they lose this distinctive savor by conforming to the world, they become useless. The image presumes a real giving of self—as the widow gave her last meal—so that grace may flavor and illumine all things.

patristicQuotes.quote: The Apostles are preachers of heavenly things, and thus, as it were, salters with eternity; rightly called the salt of the earth, as by the virtue of their teaching, they salt and preserve bodies for eternity.

Not for your own salvation merely, or for a single nation, but for the whole world is this doctrine committed to you. It is not for you then to flatter and deal smoothly with men, but, on the contrary, to be rough and biting as salt is.
If you by whom the nations are to be salted shall lose the kingdom of heaven through fear of temporal persecution, who are they by whom your error shall be corrected?

cccReferences.title: Apart from Me you can do nothing

exegesis.thematicConnection: The Christian's saltiness is sustained, like the widow's oil, by continual reliance on God; the light disciples shed echoes the psalm's plea that the light of God's face be lifted on the world.

synthesis.title: Small Things, Faithfully Given, Become Light to the World
synthesis.body: Today the Church gathers three images of grace working through what seems too little. A starving widow of Zarephath has only a handful of meal and a little oil, yet because she trusts the prophet's word and gives first to God, her jar does not empty until the rains return. The psalmist, surrounded by those who chase futile things and ask 'What can bring us happiness?', confesses that the Lord has put into his heart a deeper joy than any harvest can give—and pleads that the light of God's face shine upon His people. Then Jesus, on the mountain, turns to His disciples and tells them what such trust makes of a person: salt that preserves a decaying world, a city set on a hill, a lamp that cannot be hidden. As Chrysostom reminds us, this is not for our salvation alone but for the whole world. And as Augustine warns, salt that fears the world and loses its savor is good for nothing. The widow's secret, the psalmist's joy, and the disciple's mission are one: when we give the Lord even our last scrap with confidence, He multiplies it into nourishment and light for others. The Eucharist we receive is that same handful of bread—small, hidden, inexhaustible—making us salt and light until the rains of His coming.
